headline: CFOs can't trust probabilistic LLMs with corporate ledgers; Zero-Trust AI Gateway offers solution.
summary: Probabilistic LLMs can hallucinate math totals, posing multi-million dollar liabilities in financial systems. A Zero-Trust AI Gateway is proposed to validate AI agent outputs before they interact with ledgers, ensuring financial accuracy.
details: Probabilistic models (LLMs) are excellent at text extraction but occasionally hallucinate math totals. In financial systems, even a 1% error rate can translate into a multi-million dollar liability, making direct AI interaction with ledgers a significant risk.

The proposed architecture includes an AI Workforce Layer designed for high-speed data extraction, reading messy PDFs, parsing line items, and structuring JSON payloads from various financial documents.

A critical Gatekeeper Layer, implemented as a Node.js validation proxy, sits between the AI agent and the database or ERP. This hard rule ensures no AI agent ever touches a ledger directly, channeling every request through the gateway.

Deterministic Math Reconciliation is a core function, re-calculating subtotals, tax rates, and individual line items to the exact cent. This process guarantees precision before any transaction is executed.

An Automated Circuit Breaker provides immediate security by freezing execution if a severe variance or potential fraud vector is detected. This proactive measure prevents erroneous or malicious transactions from proceeding.

For auditing purposes, every verified transaction is locked into an unalterable, append-only state chain using a Cryptographic SHA-256 Ledger. This ensures transparency and integrity of financial records.

This comprehensive Zero-Trust AI Gateway mitigates the inherent risks of AI in finance. It transforms AI agents from a scary security risk into a controlled, safe, and highly valuable operational asset for corporate ledgers.

headline_marked: [[Android phones finally back up local documents]] to Google Drive with new feature rollout
headline: Android phones finally back up local documents to Google Drive with new feature rollout
summary: This long-awaited feature backs up PDFs, documents, and other local files, but it counts against your Google Drive storage and doesn't sync changes.
details: Google is widely rolling out a new auto-backup feature for local documents on Android phones. This update, part of the latest Google Play Services, finally addresses a long-standing omission in Android's cloud backup capabilities.

Previously, Android's cloud backups were limited to photos, videos, contacts, and messages, leaving locally stored files like PDFs and downloaded documents vulnerable to loss if a device was damaged or reset. This new feature aims to secure those critical files.

Backed-up files are stored in a new "Android backups" directory within Google Drive. Inside, a subdirectory named after your device contains a "Download" folder with your locally saved documents and other downloaded files.

Google confirms the backup includes common file types such as .DOC, .PPT, .XLS, .PDF, and all other documents saved on your device. All data is encrypted to ensure privacy and security for your personal files.

However, there are some limitations: changes made to a backed-up document on your phone will not sync to Google Drive, and vice versa. Additionally, the feature backs up *all* locally saved documents without an option to select specific folders or exclude certain files.

Document backups occur nightly, though users can manually trigger a backup at any time. It's important to note that these document backups will count towards your Google account's overall storage quota, similar to other Drive content.

To check for and enable the feature, navigate to Settings > Accounts and backup > Google backup on your Android device. If the "Documents" option is visible, ensure it's enabled and tap "Back up now" to initiate the process immediately.
